description: Beginner-oriented style examples. Profiles are broad tendencies, not predictions for a specific bottle.
budgetGuidance: Prices vary by country, producer, vintage, tax, and point of sale. Budget labels are omitted unless a cautious, relative style-level hint is defensible; missing labels are unknown, not expensive or unsuitable.

wineStyles.name: Pinot Noir
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Often a lighter-feeling red with red-fruit character. It can be a gentle way to explore red wine structure.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Body, fruit character, and earthy notes vary with climate, producer, and oak use.

wineStyles.name: Gamay (Beaujolais-style)
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Gamay often makes fresh, fruit-led reds that can be served slightly cool. Beaujolais includes several styles, so the label matters.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: The region and production method can make the wine lighter, more structured, or more concentrated.

wineStyles.name: Merlot
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Merlot can offer ripe fruit and a rounded feel. It is not always soft or light; styles differ considerably.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Climate, blending, oak, and winemaking can change its body and tannin.

wineStyles.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Often structured, with dark-fruit character and a drying grip from tannin. The grip is a mouthfeel, not sweetness or body.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Climate, age, oak, and blending can shift fruit, body, and tannin.

wineStyles.name: Syrah / Shiraz
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Syrah and Shiraz are names used for the same grape in different places. The wine may feel rich, savory, or peppery.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Climate and winemaking create a wide range of styles; the name alone does not guarantee a flavor.

wineStyles.name: Grenache / Garnacha
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Grenache can give ripe, berry-like fruit and a generous feel, while keeping tannin less prominent than some reds.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Warmth, alcohol, blending, and growing conditions can change its weight and fruit character.

wineStyles.name: Malbec
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Often a dark-fruited red with a fuller feel. Malbec is grown in many regions, which makes its style broad.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Region, altitude, oak, and producer can change acidity, body, and tannin.

wineStyles.name: Sangiovese (Chianti-style)
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Sangiovese often combines cherry-like fruit with noticeable freshness, which can work well alongside food.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Chianti rules and individual producers allow for different blends, aging, body, and tannin.

wineStyles.name: Tempranillo (Rioja-style)
flavourNotes: sometimes vanilla or spice from oak
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Tempranillo is a key Spanish red grape. Rioja-style examples can be fruit-led or show more savory and oak-related notes.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Rioja aging categories and producer choices affect the finished style; not every bottle tastes alike.

wineStyles.name: Sauvignon Blanc
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Often fresh and aromatic, sometimes with citrus or herbal notes. Fruit aromas do not mean the wine is sweet.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Climate, harvest choices, and winemaking affect the fruit and herbal balance.

wineStyles.name: Chardonnay
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Chardonnay can be lean and fresh or richer and sometimes oak-influenced. The grape name alone does not settle the taste.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Oak, malolactic fermentation, climate, and harvest decisions can change weight and flavor.

wineStyles.name: Pinot Grigio / Pinot Gris
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Many Pinot Grigio examples are light and refreshing. Pinot Gris can also be richer or more aromatic, depending on region and producer.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: The names and styles vary by region; some Pinot Gris is fuller or made with sweetness.

wineStyles.name: Chenin Blanc
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Chenin Blanc can be made dry, gently sweet, or dessert-sweet, often with lively acidity. Check the label or ask about sweetness.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Sweetness and body vary widely by region, harvest, and winemaking.

wineStyles.name: Albariño
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Often a fresh, dry white with citrus or stone-fruit character. It is a useful style to try with seafood.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Region and producer affect the body, fruit notes, and texture.

wineStyles.name: Grüner Veltliner
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Often dry and lively, with citrus or green-fruit notes. Some examples have a distinctive peppery edge.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Body and concentration vary with growing site and producer.

wineStyles.name: Riesling (dry to sweet styles)
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Riesling ranges from dry to sweet and often has lively acidity. Look for a sweetness cue or ask someone at the shop about the bottle.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Sweetness, acidity, and aroma vary by region, harvest, and producer.

wineStyles.name: Gewürztraminer
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: An aromatic white that may smell floral or spicy. Aroma intensity does not mean the wine is sweet.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Sweetness and acidity differ between regions and bottles; check the individual label.

wineStyles.name: Dry rosé
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Rosé gets its color from grape-skin contact. A dry rosé can smell fruity without tasting sweet.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Grape, skin contact, and residual sugar vary; rosé is not one single flavor or sweetness level.

wineStyles.name: Off-dry rosé
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Off-dry means some sweetness is noticeable. This can be a friendly option if you prefer a softer, fruit-led taste.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Sweetness, acidity, and grape blend are producer-specific; verify the bottle style.

wineStyles.name: Prosecco
wineStyles.budgetNote: A broad relative hint for Prosecco DOC sparkling styles; actual prices depend on country, producer, and retailer.
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: This example is a sparkling Prosecco made mainly from Glera; the name also covers still and lightly sparkling styles. Check the label for bubble style and sweetness.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Sweetness terms, pressure, and style vary. Prosecco DOC is not a price guarantee.

wineStyles.name: Cava
grapeVariety: Often Macabeo, Xarel·lo, and Parellada; blends vary
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Cava is Spanish sparkling wine, often made by traditional bottle fermentation. Its label gives useful sweetness and aging clues.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Grapes, aging, and sweetness vary across Cava categories and producers.

wineStyles.name: Champagne Brut
grapeVariety: Often Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, and Meunier; blends vary
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Champagne is sparkling wine from the Champagne region of France. Brut is a regulated sweetness term, not a grape or a flavor guarantee.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Blend, vintage, aging, and dosage can change the style; Champagne can also be made with different sweetness levels.

wineStyles.name: Moscato d’Asti
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: A gently sparkling, sweet style that can be lower in alcohol than many table wines. Check the specific bottle label.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Aromas, sweetness, and alcohol level can vary by producer and vintage.

wineStyles.name: Late-harvest Riesling
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Late-harvest wines are made from grapes picked later, which can lead to sweetness balanced by acidity. The label may use regional terms.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Sweetness, concentration, and production methods vary; not all late-harvest wines are alike.

wineStyles.name: Tawny Port
wineStyles.beginnerExplanation: Port is a fortified wine, and Tawny Port is usually sweet with nutty, dried-fruit notes. Serve size is often smaller than for table wine.
wineStyles.variabilityNote: Age indication, blend, sweetness, and price vary; the category does not describe a specific bottle.
